Subject: Tenancy Architecture Decision — Shared Schema with Tenant IDs

To: Leadership Team
From: [Your Name]
Re: Tenancy model for next quarter's build plan

Team,

I've evaluated both tenancy options against our upcoming wave of ~180 customer workspaces and have decided we'll build on a **shared schema with tenant IDs** rather than schema-per-tenant.

**Why:**
- The security review set the same baseline requirements for either approach (documented access controls, audit logging, quarterly restore drills), so security posture wasn't the deciding factor.
- Shared schema keeps migrations, connection pooling, and cross-tenant reporting simpler, with lower ongoing operational overhead — a meaningful advantage as we scale toward 180 workspaces.
- Schema-per-tenant would require migration automation across every schema on each release, adding recurring complexity that shared schema avoids.

**What this commits us to:** Shared schema shifts more of the burden onto the application layer. We'll treat row-level security, authorization checks, and cross-tenant test coverage as first-class build items next quarter, not follow-on work.

I'll fold this into the Q[next] build plan and can walk through specifics at our next sync.

[Your Name]

---

One thing worth flagging as you scope the build plan, separate from the memo: the quarterly restore drill requirement applies to both models, but it's not equally easy to satisfy. Schema-per-tenant gets tenant-level restore/delete almost for free (restore one schema). Shared schema doesn't — you'll need to build actual tooling (scoped export/restore or soft-delete-and-purge logic keyed on tenant_id) to restore or delete a single tenant's data without touching others. If that tooling isn't already an explicit line item in the plan, it's worth adding now rather than discovering the gap during the first drill.
